request.prompt:
A straight-down plan of the same abandoned saltworks at Greyhithe, the whole site in one square frame, drawn as a designer's massing plan in the same hand and palette: roofs and open ground from directly above, no perspective, north at the top.

The site is about three hundred and twenty paces west to east and a hundred and twenty-eight north to south, on a headland with sea on the north, west and south.

West end: the shingle landing at the top, and below it the six broken evaporating pans standing in water, a large square block of them.

Middle west: a small shed on the last dry pan, and a broad cut ramp climbing east off the pans.

Middle: the works, gathered around the great square boiling house — a walled coal yard north of it, a narrow hoist tower and a long store east of that, a barrel shop, and an open yard east of the boiling house, with a barred door between the yard and the boiling house.

Middle east: the abbey precinct behind its gatehouse — a square open cloister garth with a covered walk on its north side, a chapter house, a refectory, and the church, a long rectangle running north to south, with a smaller undercroft block south of it.

East end: a long narrow path out along the headland, and at the end a walled square court with the round light tower standing in it.
request.style_note: The Saltworks at Greyhithe, in one hand throughout: a cold North Sea dusk, the sky a narrow band of pale light low in the west and dark above. One masonry everywhere — grey lias limestone laid in long thin courses, iron-stained red-brown where the sea reaches it, quoins and jambs in the same stone dressed square. One way of letting light in — tall narrow round-headed openings in a repeated rhythm, high in the wall, in the works and in the abbey alike. Slate roofs weathered near-black, salt-bleached timber, no render, no whitewash. One warm lamp burning on the headland, the only warm colour in the picture. Matte gouache on toned grey paper, restrained palette, visible dry brush, no figures, no text, no lettering. Each image is ONE single full-frame view of that place, filling the frame edge to edge: never a sheet, never a grid, never a panel, never an inset or a caption.
